prime.problem: The source's claims rule p<sub>n+1</sub> = p<sub>n</sub>/5 hides a named distribution. 'Wait for the first success' questions need a tail formula and a clear convention (trials or failures), or you end up off by one.
prime.fits: After the binomial and the Poisson: instead of counting successes in a fixed number of trials, count how long until the first one. The first-step card has already used it (the thief tries a geometric number of doors), and the negative binomial adds r of them.
expect: memorylessness: P(N ≥ m + n | N ≥ m) = P(N ≥ n)
the only memoryless distribution on the whole numbers
prime.goal: Recognise a geometric from a constant ratio, use the tail qᵏ, keep the convention straight, and explain what memorylessness buys and when it's false.

attend: Why does a constant ratio between neighbouring probabilities force a geometric, and how does normalising fix p<sub>0</sub>?
Why is 'more than one claim' simply q²?
Which convention does the claims problem use, and what would the trials convention change in the mean and variance?
Why can't the Poisson, the negative binomial with r = 2 or a binomial be memoryless?

must: Each extra count is a fixed factor q as likely as the last → pₙ = p<sub>0</sub>qⁿ → normalise: p<sub>0</sub>/(1 − q) = 1 → p<sub>0</sub> = p = 4/5
N ≥ k means the first k trials all failed → P(N ≥ k) = qᵏ → P(more than one claim) = (1/5)² = 1/25
Tails are powers of q → P(N ≥ m + n)/P(N ≥ m) = qⁿ → the past drops out: memoryless. Anything whose chance of stopping changes with time (wear-out, bounded support) fails this
elevated: numpy's geometric counts trials (smallest draw 1) → subtract 1 for the failures form → mean 1/p against q/p is the classic off-by-one
reference: the (a, b, 0) recursion pₙ/pₙ₋₁ = a + b/n
the MGF exists for t < −ln q

compress.prompt: From memory, derive the claims answer in three lines (unroll, normalise, tail), then prove memorylessness in one line.
checklist: a constant ratio q means pₙ = p<sub>0</sub>qⁿ
the tail is qᵏ: the first k trials failed
a ratio of tails is qⁿ, so the past cancels
trials form mean 1/p, failures form mean q/p, same variance q/p²

retrieve.q: Explain memorylessness in terms of tails, and why no other distribution on the whole numbers has it.
answer: P(N ≥ m + n | N ≥ m) = q<sup>m+n</sup>/q<sup>m</sup> = qⁿ
memorylessness means the chance of stopping at the next step is always p
a constant stopping chance forces the tail to be qᵏ; the Poisson, NB(r ≥ 2) and the binomial all have stopping chances that change

retrieve.q: Walk through the claims problem two ways: the complement of p<sub>0</sub> + p<sub>1</sub>, and the tail formula.
Claim counts with mean 1/4: geometric, Poisson or negative binomial? What does each assume about 'one more claim'?
answer: geometric: one claim in, the next is exactly as likely (0.2 and 0.2)
Poisson: a second claim becomes less likely (0.1198 given one)
NB(2, 8/9): in between (0.1634); real claim data usually need Poisson or NB, not a constant ratio

compare.q: One geometric wait against the sum of r of them: what changes in the mean, the variance and memorylessness?
answer: the mean and variance scale by r: rq/p and rq/p²
the MGF is raised to the r-th power
only r = 1 is memoryless: for NB(5, 0.7), P(X ≥ 1) = 0.8319 but P(X ≥ 2 | X ≥ 1) = 0.697

compare.q: Discrete memorylessness here against the exponential's in cs-9: what is the same, and what changes when time is continuous?
answer: same: the tail is a pure power or exponential, so conditioning on survival resets the clock
each is the only memoryless distribution in its own setting

predict.q: Two fair dice are rolled together each round until at least one shows a 6. What is the distribution of the number of rounds, and its mean? Commit first.
predict.answer: Geometric (trials form) with p = 1 − (5/6)² = 11/36, so the mean is 36/11 ≈ 3.27 rounds. 'No 6 this round' needs both dice to miss, so q = 25/36: the minimum of two independent geometric waits is itself geometric.

apply.task: For a die rolled until a 6 (trials convention), compute P(X > 10) exactly. Then get P(X > 13 | X > 10) two ways: as a ratio of tails from the definition, and by memorylessness. Finally run the card's simulate(1/6) and check the mean.
apply.done: P(X > 10) = (5/6)¹⁰ ≈ 0.1615. Both routes give (5/6)³ = 125/216 ≈ 0.579. The simulation counts failures, so its mean is near 5; add 1 to get about 6 trials.
apply.hint: In the trials form, P(X > k) = qᵏ: the first k rolls all missed.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the two-dice p, or that the answer is still geometric?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why a constant ratio forces qⁿ, or why memorylessness is unique to it?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: constant stopping chance → memoryless, or trials → failures (the +1 shift)?
Which real waiting time in your own work is clearly not memoryless?
What will you revisit before the negative-binomial card?
